description: Get into a push-up, lock your arms, and lean forward until your shoulders pass your hands. Your max lean hold is the test, and these five mistakes are what quietly destroy your wrist and shoulder leverage: soft elbows, sagging hips, and leaning from the toes. Take the test, then fix the leaks.

scenes.narration: Push-up position. | Top position. | Arms dead straight. | Elbows locked hard. | Body one line. | Now lean forward, | slowly, from the ankles, | shoulders traveling forward | past your hands. | Further. Further. | Stop at the lean | you can truly hold. | Start your clock | right there. | Hold it honestly. | The clock stops | at the first mistake. | An elbow softens. | The hips sag. | You tiptoe instead | of leaning. | When form breaks, | stop the clock. | That clean time, | at your max lean, | is your number. | Five mistakes | are stealing it, | and we name them | before the end. | | Mark your toe line on | the floor with tape before | you lean. | Without a mark, your feet | will migrate forward a centimeter | per attempt, shrinking the lean | while your confidence grows, and | the test will grade your | optimism. | Hands go down behind the | line, fingers spread, and the | lean is measured from that | fixed base every time. | Instruments first, ego second: the | correct order for every test | in this season, and the | one your planche will be | built on.

scenes.label: AT MAX LEAN IS THE LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Ten clean seconds at your maximum honest lean, elbows locked, hips in line, shoulders clearly past your hands, is certified planche leverage. Under four clean seconds, a mistake is ending your lean before your shoulders start their real work. Over twenty, and the tuck planche is not a dream; it is the next line in your program. Judge distance and form together: a far lean with soft elbows and sagging hips is a push-up plank with ambitions. The lean only counts at the angle your straight arms can actually afford. Add a second measurement to this one: distance. Note how far your shoulders travel past your hands at your max clean lean, in finger-widths if you must. Time tells you about endurance at an angle; distance tells you about the angle itself, and planche progress is angle progress. When the distance grows at the same clean time, your leverage genuinely improved. When only the time grows, you got better at surviving a price you already owned. Both are progress. They are not the same progress, and your program should know which one it bought.
scenes.sub: under 4 clean sec: a mistake ends it - 20+: planche path

lines: Leaning moves your weight past your hands.
Wrists and shoulders split the bill.
beats.title: PAST THE BASE, PRICES RISE

scenes.narration: The mechanism is a moving base. In a normal plank, your weight sits over your hands and the price is low. Lean forward and your center of mass travels past your base, so your wrists bend deeper under load and your shoulders must hold a straight-arm lever that gets more expensive with every inch. The front deltoid and the straight-arm chain pay the shoulder half; the wrist, bent near its limit, pays the other. Every mistake ahead either pulls your weight back over the base, bends the arm that must stay straight, or lets the hips drop out of the line the lever is priced on. Protraction is the hidden half of this mechanism: your shoulder blades must wrap forward around your ribs, pushed apart by the serratus muscles, or the straight-arm chain has no foundation. A hollow, retracted plank leaks the lean before it starts. Think of pushing the floor away until your upper back rounds slightly like a cat, while the hips stay in line. That rounded-but-level shape is not bad posture here. It is the planche's actual skeleton, and most failed leans are skeletons that were never assembled.

Here is the soft elbow, measured. Let the elbows bend a few degrees at the same lean and the hold more than doubles, because the triceps and chest, the push-up muscles, flood in to do a job the straight-arm chain was supposed to do alone. It feels like planche training. It is push-up endurance in a costume. The planche is a straight-arm skill; its entire training effect lives in tendons and shoulders learning to hold a locked lever. Every soft-elbow second is a second your planche did not get, no matter how far forward your shoulders were pointing. Tendon time is the governing law of this whole family, so hear it plainly. The straight-arm position loads the biceps tendon and the wrist's connective tissue at long lengths, and connective tissue adapts at a fraction of muscle's speed. This is why planche athletes progress in seasons and why the greedy ones collect elbow pain as their first real milestone. Your leans should feel challenging and finish fresh, never grinding. The tissue you are building does its growing between sessions, on the days you were patient enough to stop early.

The dynamic partner of the lean is the pseudo-planche push-up: hands placed by your hips instead of under your shoulders, fingers turned out, and every push-up performed at your current lean angle. It converts your static leverage into pressing strength through the same position, and it gives the straight-arm chain a moving job to adapt to. Three sets of five, at a lean you can lock, twice a week. When the push-ups at your max lean get easy, the lean itself moves forward within the month, as reliably as rent. Static holds teach position. Dynamic reps teach the position to work for a living.

The season's refrain, one last time: the load past your base is your own body, so a lighter body leans further on the same shoulders. Planche athletes are famously compact for a reason. Your frame is the specification this skill was designed around, not a handicap to apologize for. But the lean only pays in clean seconds. A skinny guy leaning on soft elbows and tiptoes is rehearsing a push-up, same as everyone. Spend your cheap leverage on locked arms and honest angles. There is a silhouette dividend at the end of this road that no mirror exercise buys. Straight-arm strength builds a specific look: capped shoulders, dense forearms, a chest that sits high because the whole front chain is tension-literate. It is the gymnast's silhouette, and it reads as powerful at any bodyweight, which is precisely the point for a man whose scale will never impress anyone. Presence is not mass. Presence is structure, and this skill builds structure in its purest form.
Lean with me. Twenty seconds at your honest max, elbows locked, body one line, breathe. The moment an elbow softens, we reset together. Go.

The five mistakes destroying your wrist and shoulder leverage. One: soft elbows, the costume change we just measured. Two: sagging hips, which breaks the line and quietly moves your weight back over your hands. Three: tiptoeing forward instead of leaning from the ankles, walking your base toward your weight instead of moving your weight past your base; mark the floor where your toes start and they may not move. Four: max leans on cold wrists, asking a bent, loaded joint for its limit unprepared; warm them every session, and sharp wrist pain means stop, not push. Five: chasing distance instead of time, leaning a centimeter further each day on collapsing form. Lean less, lock everything, hold longer. Distance is earned by seconds. Mistake four, cold wrists at max lean, is the one with a filing cabinet of physio receipts behind it, so it gets the last word. The wrist in a deep lean is a joint at end range carrying a growing share of your body, and its tissues adapt like the biceps tendon: slowly, and only when respected. Two minutes of wrist warm-up before every session, and a hard rule that sharp pain ends the day, will keep your planche career measured in years. The skill is a marathon run at a sprint's address. Dress accordingly.

beats.text: UNDER 4 CLEAN: A MISTAKE ENDS IT

scenes.narration: So, your clean number. Under four seconds: a mistake is ending your lean, and its name is on the list. Four to ten clean: the straight-arm chain is learning its trade, feed it seconds. Over ten clean at a real lean: your wrist and shoulder leverage is certified, and the tuck planche belongs on your program. Retest in thirty days, toes marked, elbows locked, first mistake stops the clock. Put your clean seconds in the comments. Just the number. The lean grades your lock, and the lock does not lie. Retest with the tape down, the same hand position, and a side camera for the elbow audit, because soft elbows are invisible from inside the lean. Grade the clean seconds and the finger-widths together. If both grew, you had the best month this skill offers. If one grew, you know exactly which quality next month is hired to build. That is the entire philosophy of this season in one verdict: measure honestly, and the measurement writes the program.

Lock the arms, lean from the ankles, buy distance with seconds. That is the whole road toward the planche. Subscribe, and bring me your new clean time in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 planche lean Mistakes That Are Destroying Your wrist and shoulder leverage
